A 27-year-old G1P0 at 12 weeks estimated gestational age presents for prenatal care. The patient says she has occasional nausea and vomiting and a few episodes of palpitations and diarrhea this last week. Physical examination is unremarkable, except for a heart rate of 145/min. Basic thyroid function tests are shown in the table below. Which of the following additional laboratory tests would be most useful is assessing this patient’s condition?
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) 
0.28 mIU/L (0.3–4.5 mIU/L)
Total T4
12 µg/dL (5.4–11.5 µg/dL)?

                    ### Question
                    A 27-year-old G1P0 at 12 weeks estimated gestational age presents for prenatal care. The patient says she has occasional nausea and vomiting and a few episodes of palpitations and diarrhea this last week. Physical examination is unremarkable, except for a heart rate of 145/min. Basic thyroid function tests are shown in the table below. Which of the following additional laboratory tests would be most useful is assessing this patient’s condition?
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) 
0.28 mIU/L (0.3–4.5 mIU/L)
Total T4
12 µg/dL (5.4–11.5 µg/dL)?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Total triiodothyronine (T3) levels
opb. Free thyroxine (T4) levels
opc. Thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) levels
opd. Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies
ope. Thyrotropin receptor antibodies (TRAb)

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with symptoms and lab findings suggestive of hyperthyroidism, characterized by low TSH and elevated Total T4. In pregnancy, it is crucial to differentiate between true hyperthyroidism and physiological changes. Free T4 levels are more indicative of thyroid function than Total T4 due to changes in thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) during pregnancy. Therefore, assessing Free T4 levels (Option B) is most useful to confirm hyperthyroidism. While Thyrotropin receptor antibodies (TRAb) can help diagnose Graves' disease, the immediate need is to confirm the hyperthyroid state, making Free T4 the priority. Evidence paths support the association of hyperthyroidism with elevated T3 and T4, but Free T4 is more reliable in this context. Other tests like TPO antibodies and TBG levels are less relevant for immediate assessment of hyperthyroid status.
